title: Giving well
hookLine: On Benefits: give freely, promptly, and without reminding (On Benefits 1.1)

lines: THE FORTY DOLLARS AT EVERY DINNER.
cards: Everyone has met this person. They lent you forty dollars in college, and somehow it comes up at every dinner since. Or the relative whose birthday present arrives with a short speech about how hard it was to find.
The gift was real. The money was real. And yet something about the way it was given turned it sour, and you'd almost rather have gone without.
Seneca noticed the same thing in Rome, and wrote one of his longest works, seven books, about this one ordinary act.

teach.h: ON BENEFITS: SEVEN BOOKS ON ONE ACT.
teach.b: First, the book. It's called On Benefits, written to a friend named Aebutius Liberalis. The Latin word is beneficium: a good deed, a favor, anything done for someone else's good.
Seneca opens by saying that among all the mistakes of careless living, hardly any is worse than this: we don't know how to give, and we don't know how to receive. Second, freely.
A favor done to get something back isn't a benefit at all, he says. It's an investment. And when people turn out ungrateful, he doesn't tell us to stop.
Even after a bad harvest, the farmer sows again.

Third, promptly. Give without hesitation, he says in book two. A favor dragged out with delays, or one the other person has to beg for, loses most of its sweetness, because asking costs people something.
An old Latin proverb, usually credited to the writer Publilius Syrus, puts it shortly: whoever gives quickly gives twice. Fourth, then forget it.
There's a law between the two people in a benefit, Seneca says: one should forget at once that he gave, and the other should never forget that he received.
Reminding someone of what you did for them is close to asking for it back.
It turns a gift into a bill. Seneca isn't asking for bigger gifts, just cleaner ones: no strings, no waiting, no speeches afterward. The forty dollars would have been a lovely gift.

how: People who read Seneca's On Benefits often take up three habits from it: give without expecting a return, give before being asked twice, and never remind the other person of the favor.

giving only to people who can repay you

games.q: a friend asks if you can help them move on Saturday. you can. what fits On Benefits?
o: say yes right away, and show up.
say maybe, and decide Friday night.
help, and remind them of it later.
games.why: give without hesitation, Seneca says: a favor someone has to wait or beg for loses most of its sweetness.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to give and keep putting off: a reply, a borrowed book, a thank-you note, an hour of help. Picture giving it quickly, without a speech, and walking away without ever mentioning it again.

wordCard.voice: Giving well. Seneca's On Benefits: give freely, give promptly, and once it's given, let yourself forget it. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from bene 'well' and facere 'to do': a good deed, Seneca's subject in On Benefits.

carryVoice: Your line: give, then forget. A gift with no speech attached stays a gift. Day five hundred twelve.
